issue: Source: "There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects." Candidate: "Faction can be cured in two ways." The object of the cure ("the mischiefs of") is dropped and the claim becomes that faction itself can be cured, which contradicts Madison's argument that its causes cannot be removed and only its effects controlled (and p12 "no cure for the mischiefs of faction"). STYLE-NOTE: mischiefs -> harms.
replacement: There are two methods of curing the harms of faction. One is to remove its causes. The other is to control its effects.

issue: Source "Evidently by one of two only." (i.e. one of only two means). Candidate "Evidently by only one of two." reads as "only one of the two, not both", inverting the point that there are exactly two possible means.
replacement: By what means can this object be attained? Evidently by one of only two means. Either the same passion or interest must be prevented from existing in a majority at the same time, or the majority, having such a shared passion or interest, must be made unable, by their number and local situation, to act together and carry out schemes of oppression. If impulse and opportunity are allowed to coincide, we know well that neither moral nor religious motives can be relied on as an adequate control. They are not found to control the injustice and violence of individuals, and they lose their effectiveness in proportion to the number of people combined, that is, in proportion as their effectiveness becomes necessary.

issue: Source: "those who are able to appreciate the importance of the markets of three millions of people ... and the immense difference there would be ...". Candidate splits the sentence and writes "Such people can also appreciate the immense difference", where "Such people" reads as the three million Americans just described, not the appreciating readers. Referent error introduced by the split.
replacement: If we remain united, we can counteract a policy so unfriendly to our prosperity in a variety of ways. By prohibitory regulations extending at the same time throughout the States, we can oblige foreign countries to bid against each other for the privilege of our markets. This assertion will not seem fanciful to those who can appreciate how important the markets of three million people are to any manufacturing nation. Those people are increasing at a rapid rate, are for the most part devoted exclusively to agriculture, and are likely from local circumstances to remain so. Nor will it seem fanciful to those who can appreciate the immense difference it would make to the trade and shipping of such a nation whether its products and returns travel to and from America directly in its own ships or indirectly in the ships of another country. Suppose, for instance, that we had a government in America capable of shutting Great Britain (with whom we have at present no treaty of commerce) out of all our ports. What would the probable effect of this step be on her politics? Would it not enable us to negotiate, with the fairest prospect of success, for commercial privileges of the most valuable and extensive kind in the dominions of that kingdom? When these questions have been asked on other occasions, the answer given has been plausible but neither solid nor satisfactory. It has been said that prohibitions on our part would produce no change in the system of Britain, because she could carry on her trade with us through the Dutch, who would be her immediate customers and paymasters for the articles needed to supply our markets. But would not her shipping be materially injured by losing the important advantage of being her own carrier in that trade? Would not the main part of its profits be taken by the Dutch as compensation for their services and risk? Would not the mere matter of freight cause a considerable deduction? Would not so roundabout a trade make it easier for other nations to compete, by raising the price of British goods in our markets and by transferring to other hands the management of this important branch of British commerce?

issue: Source: "it may be enough the subject of conjecture, to occasion the oppression of individuals". Candidate "it may be enough a matter of guesswork to cause" is ungrammatical/stilted and hard to parse; sense (assessment by guesswork enough to oppress individuals) is preserved by the suggested wording.
replacement: What will be the consequence if we are not able to take advantage of this resource to its full extent? A nation cannot long exist without revenues. Deprived of this essential support, it must give up its independence and sink into the degraded condition of a province. This is an extremity to which no government will willingly come. Revenue, therefore, must be had at all events. In this country, if the principal part is not drawn from commerce, it must fall with oppressive weight on land. It has already been suggested that excises, in their true sense, are too little in harmony with the feelings of the people to allow great use of that mode of taxation. Nor, indeed, in the States where almost the only occupation is agriculture, are the objects suitable for excise numerous enough to permit very ample collections in that way. Personal estate, as has been remarked before, is too hard to trace to be made to bear large contributions by any means other than taxes on consumption. In populous cities it may be subject to enough guesswork to cause the oppression of individuals without much total benefit to the State, but beyond these circles it must, in great measure, escape the eye and hand of the tax collector. As the necessities of the State must nevertheless be met in some way, the lack of other resources must throw the principal weight of public burdens on the owners of land. And as, on the other hand, the wants of the government can never be adequately supplied unless all the sources of revenue are open to its demands, the finances of the community under such embarrassments cannot be put in a condition consistent with its respectability or its security. Thus we shall not even have the consolation of a full treasury to make up for the oppression of that valuable class of citizens who are employed in cultivating the soil. But public and private distress will keep pace with each other in gloomy concert, and will unite in lamenting the infatuation of those counsels that led to disunion.

issue: Source "heretofore framed in America"; candidate keeps archaic "heretofore" in Publius's own prose (STYLE-NOTE: modernize 1788 diction).
replacement: 1. This objection will be fully examined in its proper place, and it will be shown that the only natural precaution that could have been taken on this subject has been taken, and a much better one than is to be found in any constitution framed in America so far, most of which contain no guard at all on this subject.

issue: Source "the portraits they have sketched" (referent of "they" left open). Candidate "the portraits these writers sketched" supplies an agent ("these writers") that has no antecedent in the paper; mild addition. Passive wording keeps the source's openness.
replacement: But it cannot be denied that the portraits sketched of republican government were too accurate copies of the originals from which they were taken. If it had proved impracticable to devise models of a more perfect structure, the enlightened friends of liberty would have been obliged to abandon the cause of that kind of government as indefensible. The science of politics, however, like most other sciences, has been greatly improved. The effectiveness of various principles is now well understood that were either not known at all, or only imperfectly known, to the ancients. The regular distribution of power into distinct departments; the introduction of legislative balances and checks; the institution of courts composed of judges who hold their offices during good behavior; the representation of the people in the legislature by deputies of their own election: these are wholly new discoveries, or have made their principal progress toward perfection in modern times. They are means, and powerful means, by which the excellences of republican government may be retained and its imperfections lessened or avoided. To this list of circumstances that tend to improve popular systems of civil government I shall venture to add one more, however novel it may appear to some. It rests on a principle that has been made the foundation of an objection to the new Constitution. I mean the ENLARGEMENT of the ORBIT within which such systems are to revolve, whether by enlarging the dimensions of a single State or by consolidating several smaller States into one great Confederacy. The latter is what immediately concerns the subject at hand. It will, however, be useful to examine the principle as it applies to a single State, which I shall do in another place.

issue: Source "less to be dreaded in the former than in the latter" (republican vs democratic government). Candidate "less to be feared in a republic." drops the comparative term; restore "than in a democracy". Term use itself is correct (republic/democracy per No. 10 definitions).
replacement: The other difference is that a republic can embrace a greater number of citizens and a greater extent of territory than a democracy can. This is the circumstance that chiefly makes factional combinations less to be feared in a republic than in a democracy. The smaller the society, the fewer distinct parties and interests it probably contains. The fewer the distinct parties and interests, the more often a majority will belong to the same party. And the fewer the individuals who make up a majority, and the smaller the area they occupy, the more easily they will concert and carry out their plans of oppression. Extend the sphere and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests. You make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens. And if such a motive does exist, it will be harder for all who feel it to discover their own strength and act together. Among other obstacles, it may be noted that where people are conscious of unjust or dishonorable purposes, distrust always restrains communication, in proportion to the number whose agreement is needed.

issue: Source "he is at liberty to exercise it"; candidate "man is free to use it" drops the word "liberty", which No. 10 develops in p3-p4. Optional restore of the idiom.
replacement: The second remedy is as impracticable as the first would be unwise. As long as human reason remains fallible, and man is at liberty to use it, different opinions will be formed. As long as a connection remains between his reason and his self-love, his opinions and his passions will influence each other, and the former will be objects to which the latter attach themselves. The diversity in the faculties of men, from which the rights of property originate, is just as insuperable an obstacle to uniformity of interests. The protection of these faculties is the first object of government. From the protection of different and unequal faculties for acquiring property, the possession of different degrees and kinds of property immediately follows. And from the influence of these on the views and feelings of their respective owners comes a division of society into different interests and parties.

issue: Source "we behold them with a mixture of regret, arising from the reflection that"; candidate "with regret mixed in, because we reflect that" is awkward.
replacement: A firm Union will be of the utmost importance to the peace and liberty of the States as a barrier against domestic faction and insurrection. No one can read the history of the petty republics of Greece and Italy without horror and disgust at the distractions that continually agitated them, and at the rapid succession of revolutions that kept them swinging perpetually between the extremes of tyranny and anarchy. If they show occasional calms, these serve only as a brief contrast to the furious storms that are to follow. If now and then intervals of happiness open before us, we look on them with a mixture of regret, because we reflect that the pleasing scenes before us are soon to be overwhelmed by the stormy waves of sedition and party rage. If momentary rays of glory break out from the gloom, they dazzle us with a brief and fleeting brilliance, but at the same time they warn us to lament that the vices of government should distort the direction and tarnish the luster of those bright talents and exalted gifts for which the favored lands that produced them have been so justly celebrated.
